extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and readers/students of poetry interested in standards for poetic quality
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying evaluative principles for judging poetry (style, imagery, diction, dramatic structure, moral effect) as discussed in a 19th‑century critical essay comparing Campbell, Crabbe, Moore, and Leigh Hunt. Emphasis is on what makes poetry effective or defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty and rare imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic lines of 'so rare and ripe a beauty' that 'challenge, as they exceed all praise' — beauty linked to beauty produces ecstatic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise passages that present concentrated, 'peerless' descriptions (example: Gertrude's childhood passage). Such occasional, intensely beautiful lines should be greeted with rapture; they supply the 'pearly dew of sensibility' on which fame may rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected conceits and artificial poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been an outcry 'against poetic diction and affected conceits' — artificial ornament and theatrical conceits are suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the critic sympathises with that outcry, it should not prevent appreciation of genuine beauty when it occurs. Excessive epigram, antithesis, or hyperbole that feels contrived is a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment and imagery as core strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may 'excel chiefly in sentiment and imagery' — these qualities are central measures of poetic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how successfully a poet evokes feeling and paints images; strength in these dimensions can outweigh other mechanical faults (Campbell is praised for these).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and selectivity of ornament (avoid lavishness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamentation should be selective; indiscriminate, perpetual display ('perpetual feast of nectared sweets') results in meretricious or effeminate verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fastidious, restrained use of imagery and metaphor rather than constant glittering devices (Moore criticised for wasteful excess and repetition). Excessive repetition and double epithets fatigue the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sensory richness with restraint (avoid cloying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overloading all senses at every moment ('an attempt to gratify every sense at every instant') cloys and fatigues the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensory detail should enliven, not overwhelm. A continual display of verbal tinsel may startle momentarily but leaves 'no trace of light or warmth behind it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of massing and continuity for larger works
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet ought to have 'principle of massing' and 'continuity' — capacity for massing, continuity, height, breadth, and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, decorative verses are insufficient for large subjects; long poems need cohesion and development (Moore 'can write verses, not a poem'). Assess continuity, unity, and sustained imaginative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of form to subject (don't make verse of mere statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's material is essentially statistical, prosaic, or 'mere matter of fact', setting it in verse is inappropriate and produces an awkward result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match subject matter to poetic treatment — do not use verse to present dry enumerations or mere facts (Crabbe criticised for putting statistics into harsh verse). If truth requires plain exposition, prefer prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to nature and truthful representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal fidelity and microscopic minuteness ('paints in words, instead of colours') are virtues when they faithfully reproduce nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value precision and faithful detail (Crabbe's success rests on exact images), but beware that an exclusive fixation on the mean, sordid, or revolting without balance can make verse repulsive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast and imaginative foil to stimulate the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast (foil) and imaginative impulse engage the reader; mere literal sameness leaves the imagination unstimulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a scene or character is set off by contrast, it becomes poetically striking (Pope's use of contrast vs Crabbe's level representation). Employ foils and contrasts to lift images into poetic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and emotional effect — poetry should kindle or uplift
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ideally strengthens 'yearnings after imaginary good' and lends wings to desire; it should not deaden or contract feelings like a 'torpedo's touch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a poem stimulates aspiration and sympathy rather than leaving the reader depressed or emotionally numbed (Crabbe's work often depresses; this is a criticism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of imagination — handle great subjects with gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must be able to treat great outlines of nature and momentous subjects without reducing them to trivial ornament ('the great becomes turgid; the pathetic insipid').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether imagery and metaphor are commensurate with the subject's scale; avoid turning grand subjects into mere 'toys' or cosmetic trinkets (example: Moore would decorate Chimboraco as a jeweller's toy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate diction, clarity, and avoidance of gratuitous repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition and unnecessary ornament (e.g., repeated words, double epithets, taut metaphors) are signs of poor taste; diction should be clear and measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note instances where repetition is elegantic vs where it is mere tautology. Sound and diction should serve meaning, not merely provide continual effect (question raised about repetition in 'Linden').

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality and lyrical spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyrical spirit and sound are important measures of a poem's quality ('Battle of Hohenlinden ... most lyrical in spirit and in sound').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poem's sonic effects, rhythm, and capacity for lyric intensity — some shorter songs may display concentrated musical power even if other elements are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral or remedial imaginative purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry that exposes the dark or painful side of life should (ideally) point beyond mere description to some remedy, moral insight, consolation, or imaginative uplift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticise works that dwell in distress without offering philosophical, moral, or imaginative counterbalance (Crabbe 'puts us out of conceit with this world' without directing to another). Poetry that leaves the reader only reconciled to fate may be judged deficient.
